posts.title: The egg gripper: eleven prototypes in six weeks
posts.excerpt: How one group taught a robot arm to be gentle.
posts.content:
The Builders group wanted an arm that could lift a raw egg. The first gripper crushed it; the second dropped it. By the fifth version they had foam pads, and by the eighth a small pressure sensor that stops the motor before it squeezes too hard.

The lesson they wrote on the whiteboard at the end: change one thing at a time, and write down every test. Two eggs were broken along the way, both on purpose.

posts.title: Build a rain gauge with your kids this weekend
posts.excerpt: A bottle, a ruler and two weeks of careful readings.
posts.content:
Cut the top off a plastic bottle, turn it upside down into the base as a funnel and tape a ruler to the side. Put it somewhere open, away from roofs and trees, and read it at the same time every morning.

After two weeks, draw a simple bar chart together. Ask your child why two days with the same clouds gave different numbers. That question is where real science starts.

posts.title: Nine prizes at the regional science contest
posts.excerpt: Our students took sensors, bridges and a rocket to the city hall.
posts.content:
Fourteen students presented eleven projects at this year’s regional science contest, and nine of them came home with prizes. The thirsty-plant sensor won the junior engineering award.

Thank you to the parents who drove, carried bridges and stayed for the long afternoon of presentations. Photos of every project are on the lab board.
